content_voiceover: This table is the one you need to memorize cold for boards, because tumor markers are how you distinguish germ cell tumor subtypes without waiting for final pathology. Start with the terminology, seminoma is the term for the testicular tumor, dysgerminoma is the equivalent tumor in the ovary, and germinoma is the term used when this same histology arises at an extragonadal site. These are all low A F P and low beta-H C G, so a germ cell tumor with unremarkable or minimally elevated markers points you toward seminoma or dysgerminoma. Yolk sac tumor is the classic A F P producer, markedly elevated A F P with a negative beta-H C G, and this is the pattern to associate with infantile sacrococcygeal tumors and testicular tumors in young boys. Embryonal carcinoma flips that pattern, it's beta-H C G dominant with markedly elevated beta-H C G and only mildly elevated A F P. Choriocarcinoma is beta-H C G positive with a negative A F P, and remember it's most often found as one component within a mixed germ cell tumor rather than as a pure entity. Mature teratoma has both markers negative, which is one reason mature teratoma is considered benign, while immature teratoma can have a mildly elevated A F P in roughly a third of cases, reflecting immature yolk sac elements. Dermoid cyst, a form of mature teratoma, is also marker negative. Polyembryoma is positive for both markers. And mixed germ cell tumor, by definition containing more than one component, has marker levels that simply depend on which components are present, so you interpret the marker pattern based on what you know or suspect about the mixture.
keypoints: Yolk sac tumor: markedly elevated AFP, negative beta-hCG
Embryonal carcinoma: elevated beta-hCG, mildly elevated AFP
Choriocarcinoma: positive beta-hCG, negative AFP; usually a component of mixed GCT
Mature teratoma and dermoid cyst: both markers negative; immature teratoma may have mild AFP elevation
keypoint_voiceover: Memorize the marker pairs, yolk sac tumor means high AFP and negative beta-hCG, embryonal carcinoma means high beta-hCG with only mild AFP elevation, choriocarcinoma means positive beta-hCG with negative AFP, and mature teratoma or dermoid cyst are both markers negative. Seminoma, dysgerminoma, and germinoma are the same histology at different sites, all low marker tumors.
